topics.title: What is the OWASP Top 10, and what is on the current list?
topics.html:
OWASP is a non-profit organisation, and the Top 10 is its awareness document: the ten most critical web application security risks, updated about every four years. It is not a standard or a certification, but auditors and security questionnaires use it as a baseline. The current version is the Top 10:2025 (the previous one was 2021).

#RiskIn one sentence
A01Broken Access ControlUsers can do or see things they are not allowed to. Now also covers SSRF.
A02Security MisconfigurationThe system could be secure, but it is set up badly — defaults, open settings, too many permissions.
A03Software Supply Chain Failures A dependency, build system or third-party script you trust is compromised.
A04Cryptographic FailuresSensitive data is not encrypted, or the encryption is weak or used incorrectly.
A05InjectionUntrusted input is executed as code or query — SQL injection, command injection and XSS.
A06Insecure DesignThe architecture itself is unsafe; correct code cannot fix a missing security requirement.
A07Authentication FailuresWeak login, no MFA, bad session handling, credential stuffing.
A08Software or Data Integrity FailuresCode or data is trusted without verification — unsigned updates, insecure CI/CD.
A09Logging & Alerting FailuresAn attack happens and nobody notices, because nothing is logged or nobody reacts.
A10Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions Bad error handling: failing open, leaking internal details in error messages.
💬 Say it like this

The OWASP Top 10 is a list of the ten most critical web application security risks. It is not a standard, it is an awareness document, but in practice it is the baseline that security reviews and client questionnaires are built on. The current version is the 2025 one.

At the top is broken access control — users doing things they should not be allowed to do. Then security misconfiguration, and a new category, software supply chain failures, which is about the dependencies and third-party scripts you trust. After that come cryptographic failures, injection, which includes XSS, insecure design, authentication failures, integrity failures, logging and alerting failures, and a second new one about bad error handling.

As a frontend developer I do not own all of them, but I touch several every week — injection through XSS, supply chain through npm packages and third-party scripts, misconfiguration through CSP and headers, and authentication through how tokens are stored.

What changed in 2025?
Two new categories — Software Supply Chain Failures and Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions. Security Misconfiguration moved up to second place, and SSRF is no longer separate; it was moved into Broken Access Control.

topics.title: Which of these can a frontend developer actually influence?
topics.html:
• A05 Injection / XSS. React escapes text in JSX by default, so the risk is dangerouslySetInnerHTML, HTML from a CMS, and href values that come from user input (javascript: links). Sanitise with DOMPurify and add a Content-Security-Policy.
  • A01 Broken Access Control. Hiding a button is not access control. Every check in the UI is only for convenience — the server must check the same rule again for every request.
  • A03 Supply chain. This is very much a frontend problem: npm packages, CDN scripts, analytics tags. Use a lockfile, run npm audit and Dependabot in CI, pin versions, use Subresource Integrity for external scripts, and be suspicious of a package that appeared last month.
  • A02 Misconfiguration. A strict CSP, security headers, no source maps in production, and no secrets in the bundle — everything in frontend code is public, including environment variables that get inlined at build time.
  • A07 Authentication. How the token is stored is a frontend decision, and the wrong choice makes every XSS much worse.
  • A10 Error handling. Do not show stack traces or backend messages in the UI; log the details, show the user a generic message.
💬 Say it like this

Some of them are backend problems, but several are directly mine. Injection, because I decide whether user content ends up in dangerouslySetInnerHTML and whether we have a Content-Security-Policy. Supply chain, because the npm tree and the third-party scripts on the page are frontend code. Misconfiguration, because headers, source maps and secrets in the bundle are my responsibility.

And I always say one thing about access control: anything I do in the UI is only user experience. Hiding a button does not protect anything, because the request can be sent by hand. The server has to check the permission again.

What does a basic CSP do for you?
It tells the browser which sources of scripts, styles and connections are allowed. Even if an attacker injects a script tag, the browser refuses to run it if the source is not allowed. It is the second line of defence after sanitising.

topics.title: Where do you store the auth token?
topics.html:
PlaceRiskVerdict
localStorageAny XSS can read it — one injected script steals the sessionAvoid for real tokens
Memory (JS variable)Safe from persistence, but lost on reloadGood for the access token
HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite cookieJavaScript cannot read it; needs CSRF protectionBest default
  • The usual setup: a short-lived access token in memory, and a long-lived refresh token in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie.
  • Cookies are sent automatically, so they need a CSRF defence: SameSite=Lax or Strict, plus a CSRF token or an origin check for state-changing requests.
  • Whatever you choose, XSS is still the real danger: if an attacker can run JavaScript on your page, they can also just use the session directly from the user's browser.
💬 Say it like this

I try not to put tokens in localStorage, because any XSS can read it and steal the whole session. My default is an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie for the refresh token, so JavaScript cannot touch it, and the short-lived access token only in memory.

Cookies are sent automatically, so then I need CSRF protection — SameSite plus a token or an origin check on requests that change data. And I always add that none of this fully saves you from XSS: if someone can run code on the page, they can act as the user anyway, so sanitising and a CSP come first.
